item.title: Number-correlated photon entanglement with a quantum memory interferometer
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Embedding off-resonant ladder quantum memory in Mach-Zehnder interferometer converts ∑nan|n⟩→∑nan|n⟩|n⟩ deterministically without optical nonlinearities. Effective number-shift infidelity is 1−F=n2/(4|α|2) under strong coherent control.

Grade 0.503 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Imogen Forbes, Vincent Boyer, Louis Edwards-Pratt, Mahirul Khan, Sougato Bose, Thomas M Hird

Figure

Schematic of quantum memory interferometer showing input signal split across dual rails, ladder memory storage/retrieval, and dark-port output of number-correlated states.

Asks

Can quantum memories mediate photon-photon interactions and deterministic number-correlated entanglement without strong optical nonlinearities?

But

Requires strong coherent retrieval control field (|α|2≫n2). Doppler dephasing lowers retrieval efficiency; assumes perfect balance to prevent dark-port leakage.

Tools

ladder-type quantum memory · Mach-Zehnder interferometer · phase-matched storage and retrieval · three-wave mixing interaction

Abstract

Strong photon-photon interactions are central to quantum optical technologies yet remain challenging to realise at the single-photon level. Here, we show how embedding a quantum memory within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer enables a coherent transformation that converts single-mode photon states into number-correlated entangled states. Using an off-resonant ladder-type atomic interaction, storage and retrieval within a quantum memory maps a single-photon excitation onto a pair of photons across distinct optical modes via a driving control field. Embedding this within an interferometer deterministically produces an effective transformation in the photon number basis: ∑_n a_n |n⟩→∑_n a_n |n⟩|n⟩ without relying on conventional optical nonlinearities. Measurement of one mode enables photonic non-demolition detection, state preparation, and frequency conversion as applications of the same underlying transformation. These results establish quantum memories embedded within an interferometric architecture as a platform for measurement-induced photon-photon interactions and the generation of Gaussian and non-Gaussian entangled states.

item.title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Memory-assisted MDI-QKD protocol via in-memory matter-photon interference halves the required quantum memories and detectors, scaling secret key rate as O(η) and surpassing memoryless benchmarks at shorter distances.

Grade 0.490 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Nicolas Gauriot, Samuel Morrissey, Paul M. Burdekin, Ilse Maillette de Buy Wenniger, Sarah E. Thomas, Ian A. Walmsley, Robert I. Woodward, R. Mark Stevenson

Figure

Secret key rate plotted against total transmission distance for memoryless, dual-memory, and single in-memory MDI-QKD protocols across memory efficiencies of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%.

Asks

Can quantum memory-assisted MDI-QKD be simplified and improved by interfering a stored matter qubit directly with a travelling photonic qubit in a single memory?

Before

Two-memory assisted MDI-QKD requires two separate memories and double the detector count, with interference performed on a conventional beamsplitter after retrieving both photons.

But

Simulations assume symmetric links and asymptotic regimes without finite-size effects. Memory lifetime of telecom-ORCA must exceed several nanoseconds via rephasing or hyperfine control to beat memoryless links.

Tools

In-memory matter-photon interference · Dual-rail atomic ensemble quantum memory · Telecom-wavelength ORCA memory · Decoy-state MDI-QKD modeling

Abstract

Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

item.title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Analytically designed six-step CCZ gate protocol operating at finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction |V|∼Ω using two Rydberg states with opposite-sign van der Waals shifts (C6rr/2π=289 GHz⋅μm6 and C6rR/2π=−281 GHz⋅μm6). Total gate time is tg=2π/Ω1+43π/V+2π/V.

Grade 0.482 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Snigdhadev Ray, Sinchan Snigdha Rej

Figure

Gate fidelity against total gate time tg, comparison with the Rydberg-antiblockade CCZ protocol across interatomic distances, and gate error (1−F‾) under thermal position fluctuations.

Asks

How can a native three-qubit CCZ gate be implemented on neutral atoms in optical tweezers when the Rydberg interaction strength is comparable to the driving Rabi frequency rather than in the strong-blockade regime?

Before

Fast Rydberg-antiblockade CCZ protocol (Su et al. 2020), which drops steeply in fidelity as interatomic distance increases.

But

Numerical master-equation simulation for 87Rb; assumes negligible exchange interaction (|J6|tg/l6≪1); thermal position fluctuations evaluated at Ta=2μK with 1000 Monte Carlo samples.

Tools

Lindblad master-equation simulation · two-level Rydberg excitation with opposite-sign interactions · Monte Carlo sampling of thermal position fluctuations · trace-preserving-operator fidelity metric

Abstract

We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.

item.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — In a Kitaev-chain quantum reservoir, protected Majorana edge modes yield retention scaling as τe∼eN/ξ, balanced by local write-read residue ℛloc∼τe−2. Interactions (U≠0) autonomously load bulk memory into edge parities via second-order Liouvillian coupling at the expense of retention.

Grade 0.451 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara

Figure

Bulk-to-edge loading W and edge retention S across chemical potential μ/t and interaction U/t, accompanied by delayed-input memory function and temporal integration test R2 showing performance gains from including the endpoint parity Pend at long timescales τtar.

Asks

Can a physical system hosting protected topological information perform reservoir computation via its bulk dynamics while retaining processed information in its protected boundary modes?

But

Numerical reservoir task simulations performed at N=10, Δ=t, and tτ=1.5; analytic linear reservoir description strictly requires U=0; requires ensemble-averaged readout without mid-circuit back action.

Tools

One-dimensional Kitaev chain model · Majorana covariance space formulation · Liouvillian Dyson expansion · Echo-state property analysis

Abstract

Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

item.title: Quantum Mpemba effect in a driven-dissipative atom-waveguide coupled system
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Local ground-state quenches at atomic array edges or internal interfaces accelerate relaxation to steady state compared to bulk quenches, mediated by boundary-accumulated superradiant modes at early times and suppressed bulk subradiant modes at late times.

Grade 0.439 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Hao-Kai Chi, H. H. Jen

Figure

Trace distance T vs time γt and subradiant mode distributions for an N=80 two-segment array. A quench at interface site j=39 crosses the trajectory of bulk quench j=20 around γt≈10, relaxing faster at late times due to low mode overlap with subradiant bulk modes.

Asks

How do boundary modes, directional dissipation, and internal interfaces influence the quantum Mpemba effect in driven-dissipative waveguide QED?

But

Weak-excitation regime restricted to collective ground state and single-excitation manifold (∑μ=1N|pμ(t)|2≪1). Born-Markov approximation. Resonant driving (δ=0) perpendicular to the waveguide (θ=π/2).

Tools

Lindblad master equation · non-Hermitian interaction matrix eigendecomposition · trace distance · chiral waveguide QED model

Abstract

The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon in which a more strongly perturbed quantum system relaxes toward its steady state faster than a less perturbed one. Here, we investigate the QME in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, we introduce a local quench by resetting a single atom to its ground state and examine the subsequent relaxation dynamics. We find that quenching atoms near the array boundaries induces faster initial relaxation through enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide, giving rise to an edge-enhanced QME. Strong directional decay further amplifies this effect by promoting the spatial accumulation of superradiant modes near the preferred boundary, leading to a skin-enhanced QME. At later times, relaxation is increasingly governed by long-lived subradiant modes localized predominantly in the bulk of the array. By coupling two atomic arrays with different interparticle spacings, we further demonstrate an interface-induced QME, where quenching an atom near the interface makes the system relax more slowly at early times but approach its steady state faster at later times, owing to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Our findings reveal how the spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation, offering potential routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.

item.title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC⁽¹⁾ in 1D
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Window propagation computes first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits at arbitrary depth in classical polynomial time with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error ε=1/poly(n). On 512-qubit Clifford circuits with 768 T-gates, mean-squared error drops from 1.97×10−2 to 1.31×10−4 as window width increases from 2log2⁡n to 5log2⁡n.

Grade 0.424 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Laura Lewis, Antonio A. Mele, Ronald de Wolf, Jarrod R. McClean, Amira Abbas

Figure

OTOC values per circuit instance and mean squared error against window width w for 80 Clifford+T circuit instances at n∈{128,256,512} qubits.

Asks

Are out-of-time-order correlators classically hard to simulate?

But

Applies strictly to first-order OTOCs in 1D; does not apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D.

Tools

window propagation algorithm · Haar-random brickwork circuits · Clifford+T circuits · two-copy operator space truncation

Abstract

Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to 512 qubits for Clifford circuits with 768 T-gates and up to 22 qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

item.title: Fe²⁺:forsterite Qubit System
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulated X and Z logic gates achieve >99.7% fidelity at 1.15 ns gate times in Fe2+:forsterite at temperatures up to 10 K. Natural tunnel splitting is Δ=0.19 K (4.040 GHz) under zero field.

Grade 0.423 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Dishaanth S. Pillai, G. M. Wysin

Figure

Gate infidelity of X and Z gates as a function of decoherence rate at T=10 K, showing infidelity remains below 10−3 at predicted direct-process relaxation rates.

Asks

Can the intrinsic zero-field splitting of a non-Kramers Fe2+ ion in forsterite host coherent qubit operations robust against thermal decoherence up to 10 K?

Before

Prior non-Kramers Fe2+ qubits (Smoleński et al.) required deliberately engineered lattice-mismatch epitaxial strain in CdSe/ZnSe quantum dots to induce degeneracy, demonstrated only spin-state characterization and optical readout, and had no coherent gate-control mechanism.

But

Theoretical simulation only; spin-phonon coupling constant GE is unmeasured; Raman and Orbach relaxation rates omitted because prefactors CR and AO are unknown; readout methods require lower temperatures than 10 K.

Tools

spin Hamiltonian diagonalization · time-dependent master equation simulation · surface acoustic wave (SAW) strain driving · Qiskit cross-validation

Abstract

Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe²⁺:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

item.title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Collective coupling near half-excitation k=N/2 scales nearly linearly with N, speeding excitation transfer, but relaxation from the additional excited qubits offsets the gain. Mechanical anharmonicity of 100kHz raises single-photon target probability from 19.6% to 99.7% for N=4 qubits, while pair-dependent qubit-qubit interactions degrade optical retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%.

Grade 0.420 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Nicolas Dirnegger, Matthew Guibord, William Munizzi, Chee Wei Wong, Prineha Narang

Figure

State populations over time during transfer from |D24,0m,0o⟩, showing suppression of multi-phonon leakage and boost in target single-photon probability with 100kHz mechanical anharmonicity.

Asks

Can a collective superconducting qubit ensemble coupled to a mechanical intermediary overcome weak electromechanical coupling to improve microwave-to-optical quantum transduction?

But

Theoretical model and master-equation simulations; assumes identical transmons and prescribed heating power-laws from optomechanical crystals.

Tools

Tavis-Cummings collective Dicke model · Auxiliary transmon Kerr-blockade · Input-output linear Langevin equations · Master equation simulation with disorder and noise

Abstract

Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and g_sm/(2π)=3.81 kHz, a mechanical anharmonicity of 100 kHz raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from 19.6% to 99.7%. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.
